sections.overview: Apocheima hispidaria is an early-spring geometrid moth described by Denis and Schiffermüller in 1775. It is known in English as the Small Brindled Beauty and in French as the nyssie hispide.
sections.identification: The male has a broad, hairy thorax, yellow-orange comb-like antennae and variable grey-brown forewings, sometimes with a darker central band. Its wingspan is about 28–35 mm. The female is brownish and wingless, so she has no wingspan; the sources reviewed give no standardized female body length, body height, width or mass. Males can be confused with the larger Pale Brindled Beauty, Phigalia pilosaria, or Brindled Beauty, Lycia hirtaria, which share a similar wing pattern or hairy thorax.
sections.habitat: It inhabits deciduous woodland and other tree-rich places, including gardens, parks and shrubland; in southern parts of its range it is more associated with upland or mountainous areas. Its European range extends from Spain through central Europe to Russia, with records eastward into the Caucasus.
sections.diet: The caterpillars feed on the leaves of several deciduous trees and shrubs rather than a single host. Records include oak, willow, birch, elm, hazel, apple and blackthorn.
sections.behavior: Adults appear very early in the year, chiefly in February and March; males come to light, while the wingless females are found crawling on tree trunks. The species is single-brooded, with occasional records extending from late January into April.
sections.reproduction: The female is wingless and stays on tree trunks during the adult flight period; the winged male is the flying, light-attracted sex. The caterpillars feed through spring and early summer. It then overwinters as a pupa before adults emerge the following year.
sections.ecology: As a larva it is a broadleaf feeder in deciduous habitats, while the adults emerge near the end of winter.
sections.conservation: The Belgian Lepidoptera catalogue describes it as fairly common nationally and reports a Least Concern assessment for Flanders in 2023. This is a regional assessment, not a global status for the species.
